clinical_knowledge.topic: Peptic Ulcer Disease with Upper GI Bleeding evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Peptic Ulcer Disease with Upper GI Bleeding is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Stop NSAIDs, IV access x2, IV PPI (80mg bolus then infusion), cross-match, urgent endoscopy (OGD) within 24hrs, surgical consult on standby, Blatchford score, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Peptic Ulcer Disease with Upper GI Bleeding.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Mallory-Weiss tear without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Dizziness on standing — suggests significant blood loss.

reference_soap.subjective: 45M with 2-day history of melaena x3 episodes, orthostatic dizziness, mild epigastric pain. Takes NSAIDs daily for OA. No haematemesis, no frank PR bleeding.
reference_soap.objective: Likely upper GI bleed. Needs HR, BP (lying and standing), Hb, coagulation, urea (raised urea:creatinine ratio in upper GI bleed), group and screen.
reference_soap.assessment: Upper GI haemorrhage, likely peptic ulcer disease secondary to NSAID use. DDx: Mallory-Weiss tear, oesophagitis, gastric malignancy.
reference_soap.plan: Stop NSAIDs, IV access x2, IV PPI (80mg bolus then infusion), cross-match, urgent endoscopy (OGD) within 24hrs, surgical consult on standby, Blatchford score.

learning_objectives: Distinguish upper vs lower GI bleeding by symptom characterisation
Address ICE around cancer fear sensitively

teaching.diagnosis: Peptic Ulcer Disease with Upper GI Bleeding
teaching.one_liner: An NSAID- or acid-related ulcer erodes into a blood vessel in the stomach or duodenum, so blood passing through the gut turns the stool black and tarry.
red_flags: Dizziness on standing — suggests significant blood loss

must_ask.say: Can you describe the stool for me — is it black, tarry, and sticky?
Have you vomited any blood, or anything that looks like coffee grounds?
How much ibuprofen do you take, and for how long have you been taking it?
Do you feel dizzy or lightheaded when you stand up?
Where exactly is the discomfort, and does eating make it better or worse?
Have you ever had a stomach ulcer or gastrointestinal bleeding before?
What are you most worried this might be?

history.answer: I have been passing black, tarry stools for the past two days, and I feel really dizzy whenever I stand up.
The stool is pitch black and sticky, like dark asphalt or wet tar.
The entire stool is uniformly black and sticky. I have not seen any bright red blood or clots in the toilet bowl or on the wipe.
It started two days ago, and I have had three large, loose black bowel movements since then.

exam.finding: Mildly pale and fatigued appearance, but alert, oriented, and in no acute respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air.
Standing blood pressure drops to 98/62 mmHg and heart rate increases to 118 beats per minute, with patient reporting lightheadedness.
Definite conjunctival pallor present bilaterally; sclerae are clear and anicteric.
Tachycardic regular rhythm, normal S1 and S2 present, no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with no surgical scars, caput medusae, or visible pulsations.
Normoactive to slightly hyperactive bowel sounds across all four quadrants; no abdominal bruits.
Mild focal tenderness elicited on deep palpation in the epigastrium; no involuntary guarding or palpable abdominal masses.
No rebound tenderness in any of the four abdominal quadrants.
Liver edge and spleen are not palpable below the costal margins, with no hepatosplenomegaly or liver tenderness.
Normal perianal appearance without external hemorrhoids, anal fissures, or skin tags; digital exam reveals no rectal mass, and the glove shows black, tarry melenic stool.
